name: Zane Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cleaning chemicals, paper towels, bin liners and floor machines for Brightway Clean Supply, which serves schools, clinics and office blocks. First thing I run a small AI model that checks which contracts renew this month and what stock we need. Then I negotiate with the chemical makers and the paper mills, and by afternoon I'm on calls with the facilities managers who actually use the stuff. It's thirty years of work and I enjoy every renewal fight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that it's honest work. If the floors are clean and the toilets have paper, I did my job. What wears me out is the hours before month-end and the feeling that my pay stopped growing five years ago. My wife Samira runs a small home daycare, so we're self-reliant, but we're never comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible. The tools I use save me time, but they don't change what people need: clean schools and clean clinics. I'd tell my friends at the mosque, don't believe the hype, keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm okay about the job but not about the money. We have about two weeks of savings. The daycare income is steady but small, and our son Idris is still finishing his apprenticeship. I'd say I'm stretched, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on the monthly renewals and use the AI tool to find savings the boss, Mr. Callahan, can see. I'd ask for a raise based on that. I'd put 100 a month into a savings account. And I'd think about building a small client list of my own, for the day that Brightway slows down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably calm. I'm a planner, and plans help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you count the days until Idris finishes. What changes for you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Idris finishes his apprenticeship as an electrician next spring. That will take 400 a month off our costs. I count the days, honestly. I'm proud of him and I'm tired of paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What red tape do you mean for Samira's daycare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the system is fine if you work. I don't blame anybody. If I'd like anything, it's less red tape for small firms like Samira's daycare, which pays more in forms than it should.

say: I'd tell friends at the mosque not to believe the **hype** and to keep working.
I'd say the system is fine if you work, but small firms need **less red tape**.
think: I'm okay about the job but not about the **money**: we have about two weeks saved.
do: Use the AI tool to find **savings** my boss Mr. Callahan can see.
Ask for a **raise** based on those savings.
Start a small **client list** of my own for the day Brightway slows down.
feel: Reasonably **calm**: I'm a planner, and plans help.

fieldNote: His job feels safe here, but a thin cushion and a son still in **training** keep him uneasy.

**Quietly** builds an exit option, a client list of his own.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to find contract savings for Mr. Callahan
Ask for a raise at the next review
Put 100 a month into a savings account
Start a private list of schools and clinics that like my service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the sharp ones win. Buying, checking, planning: those are my tools already. I'd say let people learn the machine and let the market sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be one of the people who survive, I think, because I know the tools and the customers. But the firm would need fewer buyers. A team of four could become two, and the other two aren't that adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it. I'd build a reorder agent that places routine orders for our top 60 customers, and I'd propose it to Mr. Callahan as my project. I'd learn the analytics side properly with an online course, 350, from my savings. And I'd quietly take a few facilities managers to lunch so they'd follow me if I ever moved. That's just good sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy. It's like being a good swimmer in a rough sea. You're fine until you're tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the 8 percent flag. What happened next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the agent flagged that a school contract would be 8 percent cheaper with a different supplier of floor cleaner. I took it to the boss. He said nice work. He didn't say, here's a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take managers to lunch so they'd follow you. Is that loyalty or insurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should reward that. If it takes my work and then drops me, I'd say that's just wrong. But I'd also say it's not the AI's fault. It's the people at the top.

say: I'd say this is where the sharp ones win: let people learn the machine and let the **market** sort it out.
I'd say the firm should **reward** the savings people find.
think: I'd survive because I know the tools and customers, but a team of **four** could become two.
The other two buyers aren't that adaptable.
do: Build a **reorder agent** for our top 60 customers and pitch it to Mr. Callahan.
Take a **350** online analytics course from savings.
Take a few **facilities managers** to lunch so they'd follow me.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**: a good swimmer in a rough sea, fine until tired.

fieldNote: Expects the buyer team to halve; he **believes** he survives but knows his firm doesn't reward savings.

Blames the firm's **leadership**, not the technology.

steps.text: Build a reorder agent for the top 60 customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and people should be honest: nobody knows what comes next. I'd tell my friends at the mosque and the men at work that this is the time to depend on family and faith, and to learn something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my buying job's gone by 2029. Even with the best tools, a company will do the buying with fewer people, or none. I'd be 60, with a wife who runs a small daycare and a thin cushion. That's the part that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd start my own small supply business for schools and clinics I know, working from the garage, buying from the same mills. I'd sign three clients in six months, and I'd ask Mr. Callahan to let me be a partner, not a competitor. I'd sell the second car and the old boat. I'd ask Idris, the electrician, to help with the garage setup. And I'd ask Samira to expand the daycare by two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I'd like to think I could keep my head. Hands move faster when they're busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ninety days to bring in 1,500. What would make or break that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira and I would sit at the kitchen table with a pen. If my pay stops, the daycare gives us 1,900 a month. Our bills are 3,400. So I'd have 90 days to bring in 1,500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask Mr. Callahan to be a partner and not a competitor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the speed that's the problem, and I'd say governments and corporations should have been honest. But I'm not waiting for them. I'd rather build my own thing and risk it.

I'd say governments and corporations should have been **honest**.

fieldNote: Expects his job to go and the **household** gap to be 1,500 a month, so alarmed even though he sounds composed.
**Responds** by starting a business rather than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I like better. It's enough time to build. I'd tell the men I know: use the time. Learn the machine, save money, and put your family in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I could be running a small firm of my own by then, serving ten or fifteen schools and clinics. It's possible because I'm already close to the customers. I'd have a little income of my own and maybe a short stint at Brightway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year on the analytics course and building my client list. The second year, I'd start taking my first paying clients on weekends. I'd save 300 a month by cutting my own spending. I'd ask Samira about renting a small unit for the stock. And I'd train Idris on invoices so he could help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a bit of pressure. It feels like a race I can win if I start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Walk me through the primary school contract. How did you find it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first small client would be a primary school that already trusts me. A 6,000 yearly contract gives me maybe 600 in margin. It's tiny, but ten of those is a real income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave Brightway early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brightway lets me go early, I'd still have my own thing. If it doesn't, I'd keep both for a while. I'm not ashamed to hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say, is a good deal for a man of my age. I'd tell younger men to take it as a gift and build something real. I'd also say not to wait for anyone to hand you a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68. I'd probably still be working part-time, running a small supply business with a couple of employees, maybe Idris. I think the thin savings would be fixed by then. I'd feel secure enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools fully, work at Brightway until 63 or 65, and grow my own clients. I'd save 250 a month, buy my son a van to start his own electrician business, and keep Samira's daycare going. I'd tithe what I can and look after my parents. And I'd vote for lower taxes on small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud of myself for being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a person who knows customers has an edge. How long would that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd watch is whether my small firm can be undercut by a big firm with its own agents. That's the real risk. But a trader who knows the customers always has an edge, even against a big firm with its own agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a van for Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask government to leave small firms alone and fund apprenticeships. I'd ask big companies to hire the young. If they do that, I'd call it fair.

I'd say leave small firms alone and fund **apprenticeships**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, I'm 60, and the daycare covers little more than half our bills. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small firms, honest warnings from companies, and apprenticeships for young people. And a bit of luck with the first three clients.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that men my age aren't finished. Some of us are ready to start again. We just need a fair field and a bit of time.

headlineQuote: Men my age aren't finished. Some of us are ready to start again. We just need a fair field and a bit of time.
portrait: **Zane Usman**, 58, buys cleaning supplies for a distributor serving schools and clinics, and uses AI tools every day.
He is **traditional** and adaptive: faith, family and free markets shape him, and he prefers building his own thing to waiting.
A thin cushion and a small daycare income keep him **uneasy**, and **alarmed** when he expects the buyer job to go.
He plans a small supply business, a client list and a hedge between Brightway and his own firm.
He blames leadership and slow governments, not the technology.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because the daycare covers little more than half the bills and the job could go.
whatWouldHelp: Lower taxes and less red tape for **small firms**, honest warnings and apprenticeships.
A little **luck** with his first three clients.
